title: Pipelines and hazards
subtitle: Overlap the stages of consecutive instructions like an assembly line — then deal with the times one instruction needs another’s result.

idea.title: The assembly-line idea
idea.body: An instruction needs fetch (IF), decode (ID), execute (EX), memory (MEM) and write-back (WB). Done one at a time, four instructions take 20 cycles. Pipelining starts the next instruction as soon as the first leaves IF, so a new instruction completes every cycle once the pipe is full. Latency of one instruction is unchanged; throughput improves by up to the number of stages.
idea.steps: k = 5 stages, n = 100 instructions, no stalls. First result after k cycles, then one per cycle: k + (n − 1) cycles. Unpipelined: n·k. Speed-up.

hazards.title: Hazards
hazards.body: A hazard stops the next instruction from proceeding. Structural: two instructions need the same hardware (one memory port for instruction and data). Data: an instruction needs a result not yet written (lw r1… then add r3,r1,…). Control: a branch changes the next fetch address before it is known. The cure is to stall (insert bubbles), forward results early, or predict.

forward.title: Forwarding and stalling in numbers
forward.body: Dependent ALU instructions back-to-back, no forwarding: the consumer must wait until the producer has written the register file, costing 2 bubbles. With forwarding: 0. A load followed by its consumer: 1 bubble even with forwarding. Toggle the two cards above and count the clock numbers to check.

branch.title: Branches and the RISC pipeline
branch.body: Until a branch is resolved the fetch unit does not know which instruction is next. Options: stall until resolved; predict not taken and flush if wrong; branch delay slot (execute the following instruction regardless); or dynamic prediction with a history table, which is right over 90% of the time on real programs. A wrong guess flushes the instructions fetched since the branch, costing their cycles.
branch.steps: 20% of instructions are branches, 30% of them mispredicted, each mispredict costs 2 cycles. Extra CPI = 0.2 × 0.3 × 2.

vector.title: Parallel and vector processing
vector.body: SIMD / vector machines apply one instruction to many data items at once (adding two vectors of 8 numbers in one step); superscalar CPUs issue several instructions per cycle; memory interleaving spreads consecutive addresses over several banks so a vector can be fetched one element per bank per cycle. Matrix multiplication is the classic beneficiary: each row-column dot product is independent.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Pipelining raises throughput, not latency.
  • Hazards: structural, data, control; fixes: stall, forward, predict.
  • CPI = 1 + stall cycles per instruction.
